result.title: Why are electric vehicles still the ‘car of the future’?
result.description:
They are cleaner, quieter and cheaper to run. So why is the transition to electric cars taking so long?
Electric vehicles are an important part of the energy transition, and are increasingly attractive to consumers as petrol and diesel prices rise. But in Europe and North America, they are still a minority of cars on the road.
On this episode we ask why that is, and what is needed to accelerate the move to cleaner mobility.

Hosts:
Robin Pomeroy, host, Radio Davos
Laia Barbarà, Director, Clean Mobility and Infrastructure, Centre for Nature and Climate, World Economic Forum
Guests:
Agustin Delgado, Chief Technology Officer, Iberdrola
Elaine Buckberg, Senior Fellow, Harvard University, Salata Institute for Climate and Sustainability and the Belfer Center
Paul Farrell, Chief Strategy Officer, BorgWarner

result.title: This MRI scanner comes to patients
result.description:
Meet the MRI scanner that can go anywhere - on the back of a truck.

Standard MRI scanners weigh up to eight tonnes and are filled with around 1,500 litres of super-cold liquid helium. They’re expensive, hard to transport, and rely on a scarce and finite resource. 

Meanwhile, studies have found that two-thirds or more of the world population do not have access to MRI, leaving them without the benefits of earlier disease detection, more accurate diagnoses and better outcomes.

This new micro-cooled MRI scanner uses less than 0.5% as much helium, and is designed specifically to be loaded onto a truck and delivered to patients in remote places.

Here, Roy Jakobs, CEO of Philips, explains how it works.

result.title: How the 1985 Mexico City earthquake shaped this architect’s career
result.description:
Antonio Gómez-Palacio, Partner and Chair of design practice Dialog, was a teenager when a huge earthquake struck Mexico City in 1985. He saw first-hand the scale of destruction, and watched as the city rebuilt itself in the years that followed.

Only much later, he says, did he realise that this had been a formative experience in his choice of career as architect and urban planner. It has also informed the way he understands and responds to the biggest challenges facing #cities and their inhabitants today: affordability, social inequality and #climate change.

result.title: What Successful CEOs Do Differently During Transformation: Real World Case Studies
result.description:
More than 70% of leaders believe their organizations could become extinct within 10 years without the right transformation. Yet fewer than 30% surveyed believe they are good at making those changes happen. So what separates the successful changes from the stalled initiatives?
Constantine Alexandrakis is the CEO of leadership consultancy Russell Reynolds Associates. In his book The Catalyst CEO, he compiles stories and practical lessons from real CEOs and their change stories, breaking down what’s needed to make change possible, especially as leadership evolves in an AI era. He shares practical lessons from companies such as Eli Lilly, Merck and Yum Brands and organizational blindspots you can’t ignore. He also shares his own his hard-won transformation story as well as the importance of ‘philotimo’ that can build a sense of stewardship in leaders.

In this episode, you’ll learn:
Why driving change is challenging - and what leaders overlook
How learning sharing power can strengthen empowerment and speed change
What is psychological inertia and how it can slow transformation
How to spot and tap ‘influencers’ in your team 
The shocking announcement that kicked off one company’s leadership restructure
The value satire plays after big changes - and why it’s an unsung form of feedback

Alexandrakis also discusses AI, distributed leadership, psychological inertia, the meetings he never skips, and gives his take on big trends shaping the future of work.

Subscribe to Meet The Leader on Apple, Spotify or YouTube.
